dct_description_sm: This study is part of the ADAPT project (Arctic Development and Adaptation to Permafrost in Transition). The observations of deteriorating conditions of inland water at temperate latitudes give rise to the question: what will be the effect of accelerated global warming and associated landscape changes on the quantity and quality of high latitude freshwaters? This research on permafrost thaw ponds addresses the hypothesis that this abundant class of aquatic ecosystems may become prone to bloom-forming cyanobacteria, with implications for water quality and food webs. In order to approach such a broad problem, multiple dynamic processes influencing the plankton dynamics need to be studied and following specific questions need to be answered: what are the bottom-up and top down factors shaping cyanobacterial communities in Subarctic ponds and are the communities of planktonic cyanobacteria in Subarctic ecosystems driven by differences in location, geological past and limnological properties. To evaluate the hypotheses listed above, study goals are: I.to characterise the planktonic cyanobacteria communities in Subarctic thaw ponds and to characterise the physicochemical, biochemical and ecological parameters driving the population dynamics of planktonic cyanobacteria.  II.to understand the effects of temperature and nutrient availability on the phytoplankton growth in Subarctic ponds.  III.to characterise the zooplankton communities in Subarctic thaw ponds and to determine experimentally the nutritional value of picocyanobacteria for Daphnia pulex isolated from thaw pond.
dct_title_s: Ecology of planktonic cyanobacteria in Subarctic permafrost thaw lakes (Whapmagoostui-Kuujjuarapik, Nunavik)
